# Kumbhajātaka (Ja 512)

**ID:** Ja 512
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Kumbhajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Sin Within the Cup
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja512
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul15.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kumbhajātaka* (Ja 512) is a canonical Jātaka tale centered on the origin and catastrophic consequences of intoxicating drink. According to its framing narrative, the Buddha recounted the story while residing at Jetavana after Visākhā questioned him about the origins of liquor, following an incident where five hundred of her female companions drank strong drink and misbehaved [SuttaCentral; Burlingame 1921; Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003]. The embedded story of the past explains that fermented fruit juice was first discovered in a hollow tree by a forest dweller; as drinking spread, it threatened the ruin of all India until Sakka (Śakra), king of the devas, intervened by appearing before a king with a jar to deliver a stern discourse on the ruinous consequences of alcohol [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003; Anderson 1978]. In his study of early trade and culture, Laufer notes from the Jātaka's account that *surā* was prepared from rice [Laufer 1919].

Scholars have analyzed both the literary composition and artistic transmission of the narrative. Winternitz observed that the canonical core consists essentially of ancient gnomic verses portraying the frightful evils of liquor to edify a monarch, while the narrative surrounding the discovery of drink is commentary [Winternitz 1933]. In Buddhist art, the story is depicted on later reliefs at Bodh Gayā, which illustrate Śakra holding a jar and dissuading the king from indulgence [Anderson 1978]. The tale was adapted into Sanskrit as the seventeenth narrative of Āryaśūra's *Jātakamālā* [Martin 2006; Dimitrov et al. 2002; Speyer 1895]. Āryaśūra's verses on the ironical praise of alcohol subsequently served as the direct source for the fourth chapter of Sajjana's *Putralekha*, preserved in Tibetan [Martin 2006; Dimitrov et al. 2002]. SuttaCentral also notes that the text is cited in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 1.1) [SuttaCentral].

DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse between the verse text and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (154 matching segments), as well as citations in modern exegetical works by Leḍī Sayāḍo (*Paramatthadīpanī* and *Anudīpanīpāṭha*) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-linguistically, DharmaNexus aligns the Pali text with 26 segments of the Tibetan *Putralekha* (D4187), matching the parallel text transmission established by modern philology, and detects partial alignments with the *Ārya-saddharmānusmṛtyupasthāna* (D0287) [DharmaNexus; Dimitrov et al. 2002].

- [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003] Nyanaponika Thera, Hellmuth Hecker, and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha: Their Lives, Their Works, Their Legacy (2003) — Provided summary of the narrative plot involving Visākhā, fermented hollow-tree juice, and Sakka's intervention.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, History of Indian Literature, Vol. II: Buddhist Literature and Jaina Literature (1933) — Analyzed the structure of Ja 512 as an ancient verse collection of moral sayings on the evils of drink.
